blogs.title: Fair Use at the Pleading Stage: Why Santos v. Kimmel Matters Beyond Late-Night TV
blogs.description: This post would examine the Second Circuit’s readiness to affirm dismissal on fair-use grounds at Rule 12(b)(6), emphasizing its reliance on the complaint, the registered works, and the segments themselves. It would situate the decision alongside TCA Television, Cariou, Hachette, and other Second Circuit cases that treat fair use as resolvable early when transformation and lack of substitution are apparent, and ask what this means for plaintiffs hoping to survive to discovery.

blogs.title: After Warhol, Purpose Is Objective: Santos v. Kimmel and the Limits of ‘I Meant It That Way’
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s treatment of transformative purpose after the Supreme Court’s Warhol decision. The key move was rejecting Santos’s argument that Kimmel ‘designed’ the original videos and therefore shared their purpose; instead, the court asked what a reasonable observer would think the videos were for. The post would explore how this objective approach affects commissioned works, prompted speech, parody, and cases where the defendant obtains the work through deception.

blogs.title: No Cognizable Market for Lampooning: The Fourth Factor in Santos v. Kimmel
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s handling of market harm, including its insistence that criticism and mockery may devalue a work or a persona without usurping any legitimate copyright market. Drawing on Campbell and Hachette, it would explain why the court treated full use of the Cameo videos as compatible with fair use once the use was commentary rather than substitution, and why a copyright owner cannot manufacture a licensing market for being criticized.

blogs.title: When Platform Rules Don’t Travel: Third-Party Beneficiaries, Implied Contracts, and Fraud After Santos v. Kimmel
blogs.description: This post would leave copyright aside and unpack the state-law holdings. It would explain why Santos could not enforce Cameo’s Terms of Service as a nonparty under Illinois law, why his implied-contract theory failed under New York pleading standards, and why his fraudulent-inducement claim collapsed for lack of out-of-pocket loss. It would also note the panel’s decision not to resolve copyright preemption, highlighting a practical lesson for creators who assume platform terms give them enforceable control over downstream uses.
